messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 78
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: European
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Graphic Designer
- Trauma Type: Natural disaster
- Pcl5: 43

She is seventy-eight now, a European woman with a careful eye for color and balance, still working as a graphic designer from the sunroom she and her husband converted into a studio years ago. Even before she tells the story directly, it comes through in the way she arranges things in the office: her handbag placed square to the chair leg, her scarf folded twice before setting it down, her gaze drifting toward the window whenever the wind rises. She says she has always liked structure. Since the storm, structure feels less like a preference and more like a lifeline.

The disaster happens six years earlier, in the small coastal town where she and her husband have lived since retirement age, though she never truly retired. She continues taking on design commissions—museum brochures, wedding invitations, logos for local businesses—pleased by the quiet discipline of choosing a typeface, adjusting white space, making something coherent. In the days before the storm, she follows the forecasts but does not fully believe the warnings. She has lived through bad weather before. She stocks canned food, fills containers with water, moves some artwork from the lower shelves, and prints out a client proof before the electricity becomes unreliable. She remembers feeling faintly foolish, as if she is overreacting.

By the night it hits, the house no longer feels familiar. The wind screams so loudly she cannot hear her husband unless he is right beside her. Rain comes in under the doors and through the seams of the old window frames. At some point the lights fail, and the rooms become a confusion of flashlight beams, banging shutters, and the groan of the roof under pressure. She stands in the hallway in her nightgown, clutching a folder of important papers against her chest, absurdly protective of passports, insurance forms, and two printouts of incomplete design drafts. When the back window shatters, she freezes. Her husband pulls her toward an interior closet, and they crouch there for hours while the house seems to shake apart around them. She is certain, in those moments, that they are going to die. What she remembers most clearly is not one image but a sensation: helpless waiting, with no action left to take.

In the aftermath, the neighborhood looks stripped raw. Trees are split open, roofs peeled back, cars tipped at strange angles as if placed by hand. Their home is still standing, but water has soaked the floors and climbed the walls, leaving a dark line she cannot stop staring at. The studio is ruined. Portfolios swell and buckle; paper fuses together; sample books bloom with mold. She tries to sound practical when she describes this part, but her voice changes when she says, “My work was floating.” For months afterward, she cannot throw anything away without feeling she is abandoning evidence of what happened.

At first, she assumes the fear will fade once the repairs are finished. Instead, it follows her into ordinary life. Rain on the roof makes her chest tighten before she has consciously noticed the weather. If the wind picks up at night, she stays dressed, shoes on, listening. She checks the emergency bag repeatedly—flashlights, batteries, medications, copies of documents—sometimes three or four times in an evening. Her husband tells her they are prepared, but reassurance never lasts. She says she feels embarrassed by how quickly she goes “from calm to terror,” as if some internal switch has been damaged.

Sleep becomes thin and unreliable. She startles awake with the conviction that she has heard glass breaking. Some nights she dreams of water rising silently through the house; on others she is back in the closet, unable to move, waiting for the walls to give way. In the morning she often feels already exhausted, as though she has spent the night on watch. She becomes irritable in ways that surprise her. A dropped pan, a weather alert on television, even her husband asking an innocent question while she is checking forecasts can make her snap. Afterward she feels ashamed and withdrawn.

Her work changes too. She still meets deadlines, but every commission takes longer. Before the storm, she enjoys experimentation; now she finds herself overcontrolling details, unable to stop revising. She avoids taking projects from clients near the coast because she does not want to drive past streets that still hold broken images in her mind. She no longer uses certain shades of gray-green in her designs because they remind her of the sky that afternoon. During storm season she keeps the radio on low all day, monitoring weather updates while pretending to work. When clouds gather, she cannot concentrate on fonts or layouts; she begins moving objects off the floor, charging devices, checking windows, rehearsing exit plans.

She says the hardest part is that the world no longer feels dependable. She used to experience home as a place that held her life together—her marriage, her work, the routines she prized. Now safety feels provisional, something that can be revoked without warning. She knows, rationally, that not every storm becomes a catastrophe. But in her body, every darkening sky carries the old certainty that disaster is already underway. Even in the bright order of her restored studio, with paper swatches lined up and drafts pinned neatly to the board, part of her remains in that interior closet, listening for the sound of the house giving way.
